source_text:
Ad Xystum episcopum Romae
EPISTOLA LIII. CYRILLI AD SANCTUM XYSTUM PAPAM.
Κυρίλλου ἐκ τῆς πρὸςἸούστον [ξορρ. Ξύστον] ἐπίσκοπονῬώμης
ἐπιστολῆς.
Ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε ἐλέγχομαι πεφρονηκὼς ἕτερόν τι πώποτε παρὰ τὸ δοκοῦν τῇ
ἀληθείᾳ, οὔτε παθητὴν εἴρηκά ποτε τὴν θείαν τοῦ Λόγου φύσιν. Καὶ μετὰ βραχύ·
Οἶδα δὲ καὶ ἀπαθῆ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ φύσιν καὶ 77.288 ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον, κὰν τῇ
τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος φύσει, καὶ ἕνα ἐν ἀμφοῖν καὶ ἐξ ἀμφοῖν τὸν Χριστόν.
pass_a_gloss: Lemmatic heading naming Cyril and his letter to Justus, bishop of Rome, with a corrector note changing Justus to Xystus. Cyril then defends his record on two counts: no one has ever caught him entertaining a view that clashes with what truth itself endorses, and at no point has he described the Word in his divine being as open to pain. After a short gap in the quotation he adds that he recognizes the being of God as closed to pain, fixed, and immune to alteration, even where it meets the human frame, and he confesses a single Christ who abides within each of the two frames and derives from each of them.
pass_b_english: From the letter of Cyril to Justus (read Xystus), bishop of Rome.
For I have never been shown to have held any belief at odds with what the truth approves, nor have I ever called the divine nature of the Word capable of suffering.

And a little further on: I know too that the nature of God is incapable of suffering, unchangeable, and unalterable, even in the human nature, and that Christ is one, in both natures and from both natures.

lemmas.gloss: I am convicted, refuted, shown up

choices.issue: Garbled corrector note [ξορρ. Ξύστον] in the heading
choices.choice: Read ξορρ as corr. (corrige): the addressee Justus should read Xystus; rendered as a parenthetical aside.

Even in the human nature: the divine nature stays impassible in union with the humanity.
